question: to the Commission Jorge Martín Frías (PfE) Subject:

In its communication on the Critical Raw Materials Act, the Commission highlights the strategic role of minerals such as lithium and rare earths for green transition technologies, including wind energy, photovoltaics and batteries. At the same time, the Commission itself and the Council recognise that nuclear energy is essential ‘to achieve the Union’s decarbonisation objectives’, as well as its security-of-supply objectives. However, radioactive minerals used as nuclear fuel – being the jurisdiction of the Euratom Treaty and the Euratom Supply Agency – fall outside the scope of the Critical Raw Materials Act. In view of the above: 1.
How does the Commission ensure that nuclear fuel supply chains receive equivalent regulatory treatment to critical raw materials linked to renewable energy?

Does it intend to propose, under the Euratom Treaty, a specific instrument establishing security-of-supply and diversification objectives for radioactive minerals that are similar to those set out in the Critical Raw Materials Act?
What does it assess is the impact of that regulatory asymmetry on the technological neutrality proclaimed in the European Green Deal?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (12.6.2026) The Commission has a longstanding policy of treating nuclear fuels as critical for energy security through a comprehensive and coordinated policy approach that addresses the strategic importance of nuclear energy for EU security of supply, as underlined in the Energy Union Strategy1 and the European Energy Security Strategy2. In May 2025, the Commission adopted the REPowerEU Roadmap3 towards ending Russian energy imports4. The Roadmap outlines future actions to support the gradual phasing out of nuclear material supplies from Russia, and the ramp-up of EU alternative capacity in the nuclear fuel cycle. Together with increased cooperation between the EU and reliable international partners, this is necessary to ensure a resilient EU energy system. The EU aims to ensure access to nuclear-energy materials for all countries within the European Atomic Energy Community. Uranium is not included in the Critical Raw Materials Act5, as the Commission closely monitors the supply of nuclear materials, including uranium, under the dedicated and well-established Euratom legal framework6. Consequently, the Commission has no current plans to propose a dedicated instrument mirroring the Critical Raw Materials Act for radioactive minerals. The global market for the supply of natural uranium7 is presently diversified. The Commission is also monitoring the supply of other materials used in nuclear fuel components8.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex:52015DC0080. 2 Which establish that diversification of energy sources, suppliers, and routes is essential for ensuring secure and

resilient energy supplies. See: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legalcontent/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A52014DC0330&qid=1777045916011. 3 https://commission.europa.eu/topics/energy/repowereu_en. 4 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legalcontent/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A52025DC0440R%2801%29&qid=1747125158211. 5 https://single-market-economy.ec.europa.eu/sectors/raw-materials/areas-specific-interest/critical-rawmaterials/critical-raw-materials-act_en. 6 Namely the Euratom Treaty and the Euratom Supply Agency (ESA), which provides instruments to monitor supply, support diversification and safeguard security of supply for fissile materials. 7 Which is the main fissile material used in nuclear power plants. 8 Such as zirconium, which is equally mined in sufficient quantities, or gadolinium (listed under heavy rare earth elements) or beryllium, graphite or vanadium, which are already listed in the Critical Raw Materials Act Annex II.
